procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Sessions Judge, Court No.3, Kannauj
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 02.09.2014 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Government Appeal No. 3317 of 2014.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State of U.P. filed an application for leave to appeal before the High Court under Section 378 (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, against the acquittal of the respondents by the trial court. The High Court declined to grant leave and rejected the application. The High Court's order was unreasoned, lacking facts, submissions, findings, and reasons for declining leave.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of U.P. filed a special leave petition in the Supreme Court (Criminal Appeal No. 1094 of 2018) against the High Court's order. The Supreme Court granted leave, observed that the High Court erred in passing an unreasoned order, disapproved of the High Court's casual approach, and remanded the case to the High Court to decide the application on merits, uninfluenced by the Supreme Court's observations. The Supreme Court clarified that it had not applied its mind to the merits of the case.

directions: The case is remanded to the High Court.
The High Court will decide the application on merits uninfluenced by any of the observations made in this order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court is obligated to provide a reasoned order when deciding on an application for leave to appeal against an acquittal.

facts: The State of U.P. filed an application in the High Court for leave to appeal against an order of acquittal passed by a lower court.
The High Court rejected the application with a brief order, stating that there was no merit in the application and that the view taken by the trial judge was not perverse or unreasonable.
The High Court's order did not set out the facts, the submissions of the parties, or provide specific reasons for its conclusion.
The State appealed this dismissal to the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court's order was bad in law because it was unreasoned.
law: Under Section 378(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an appeal against an acquittal can only be entertained with the leave of the High Court.
When deciding whether to grant leave, the High Court must apply its mind to the case and consider whether a prima facie case has been made out or if arguable points have been raised.
The appellate court is obligated to record reasons, even if brief, for its decision to refuse leave to appeal. This demonstrates that it has considered the relevant material and testimonies.
If the material on record discloses arguable points that require deeper scrutiny or re-appreciation of evidence, the appellate court must grant leave and decide the appeal on its merits.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had "grossly erred" by passing the order without assigning any reasons.

It characterized the High Court's order as a "clear case of total non-application of mind" because it failed to set out the facts, submissions, findings, or the reasoning behind its decision to deny leave.

The Court noted that the High Court did not properly engage with the case; it neither found that the case required a full hearing (by granting leave) nor did it provide a reasoned justification for refusing leave.
This casual approach was held to be against the law laid down in previous Supreme Court decisions, such as *State of Maharashtra vs. Sujay Mangesh Poyarekar*.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the State's appeal, holding that the High Court is obligated to provide a reasoned order when deciding an application for leave to appeal against an acquittal. The unreasoned order of the High Court was set aside, and the matter was remanded to the High Court for a fresh decision on the application, to be decided on its merits and in accordance with the law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court is obligated to provide a reasoned order when deciding on an application for leave to appeal against an acquittal.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred by dismissing the application for leave to appeal with an unreasoned order.
respondent_arguments: The text does not contain the arguments of the respondent.

cases.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Sujay Mangesh Poyarekar
cases.principle: The High Court must provide reasons when deciding an application for leave to appeal and cannot dismiss it with a cryptic, unreasoned order.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In deciding whether to grant leave to appeal an acquittal, the High Court must apply its mind to consider if a prima facie case has been made out or if arguable points have been raised, rather than determining if the order of acquittal would ultimately be set aside.
obiter: It cannot be laid down as an abstract proposition of law of universal application that each and every petition seeking leave to appeal against an order of acquittal must be allowed by the High Court and appeal must be admitted.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While it is not an inviolable rule that every application for leave to appeal an acquittal must be granted, the appellate court is obligated to apply its mind to the material on record. In cases where it refuses leave, it must record reasons, even if brief, explaining why leave should not be granted. The High Court in this instance failed to do so, as it neither properly considered the matter nor provided reasons for its refusal.
legal_tests_applied: When deciding whether to grant leave to appeal an acquittal, the High Court must apply its mind to consider whether a prima facie case has been made out or if arguable points have been raised, not whether the acquittal would ultimately be set aside.
At the leave to appeal stage, the court should not enter into a detailed analysis of the evidence or refuse leave simply on the basis that the trial court's judgment was not 'perverse'.
If arguable points are raised or the material on record discloses a need for deeper scrutiny and reappreciation of evidence, the appellate court must grant leave and decide the appeal on its merits.
why_appellant_lost: The court qualified its agreement with the appellant by stating it is not an absolute rule that every petition for leave to appeal an acquittal must be allowed and decided on its merits.
policy_considerations: Requiring appellate courts to provide reasons for refusing leave to appeal an acquittal ensures there has been a proper application of mind and that potentially meritorious appeals are not dismissed without due consideration.
